title: Exception Hierarchy
summary: Master the Throwable inheritance tree: Error, Exception, RuntimeException, checked vs unchecked branches, polymorphic matching, and why catch ordering matters.
learningOutcomes: Map the Java Exception inheritance hierarchy accurately
Structure multiple catch blocks with correct specific-to-general ordering
Apply Java 7 multi-catch syntax for sibling exceptions

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Exception Hierarchy

breakdown.details: Object -> Throwable -> Exception -> RuntimeException -> Specific Exceptions.
Subclasses of RuntimeException are unchecked. Direct subclasses of Exception are checked by the compiler.
A catch block matches any object satisfying: thrownException instanceof CatchType.
Specific child exceptions must appear before general parent exceptions to avoid unreachable code compile errors.

activities.description: Demonstrates specific child catches, parent class catches, and the ultimate Exception fallback.

steps.description: catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException) matches because ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException extends IndexOutOfBoundsException.
catch (RuntimeException) catches NullPointerException since NPE extends RuntimeException.

questions.question: What happens if a developer writes `catch (Exception e)` before `catch (ArithmeticException e)` in a try-catch construct?
options: The code fails to compile with an 'unreachable catch block' error
The JVM prints a runtime warning
questions.explanation: Because ArithmeticException is a subclass of Exception, the first catch block would intercept all ArithmeticExceptions, leaving the second catch block unreachable (a compile error).

questions.question: Which of the following classes is the direct superclass of `RuntimeException`?
Which category of exceptions is NOT checked by the Java compiler at compile-time?
questions.explanation: Unchecked exceptions are those that inherit from `RuntimeException` (or `Error`). The compiler does not mandate try-catch or throws for them.

questions.question: If `Class B` extends `Class A`, which catch block must be placed first?
options: catch (A e) must be placed before catch (B e)
catch (B e) must be placed before catch (A e)
They must be combined with the & operator
questions.explanation: The more specific child class (B) must precede the more general parent class (A) so that B can catch its specific instances before A intercepts them.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException extends IndexOutOfBoundsException. The first matching catch block (`IndexOutOfBoundsException`) captures it and prints "Caught Index".

questions.question: Which of the following is a checked exception in Java?
questions.explanation: `IOException` extends `Exception` directly (not `RuntimeException`), making it a checked exception enforced by the compiler.

questions.question: Can a single catch block catch multiple sibling exceptions in Java 7+?
options: No, each catch block can only declare one type
Yes, using the multi-catch syntax: catch (ArithmeticException | NullPointerException e)
Only using commas: catch (TypeA, TypeB e)
questions.explanation: Java 7 introduced multi-catch syntax using the pipe `|` symbol: `catch (ArithmeticException | NullPointerException e)`.

questions.question: In multi-catch syntax `catch (A | B e)`, can A be a subclass of B?
options: No, alternative exceptions in multi-catch cannot be related by subclassing (compile error)
questions.explanation: If A is a subclass of B in `catch (A | B e)`, the compiler flags an error because A is redundant.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is caught by RuntimeException. Because RuntimeException extends Exception, `e instanceof Exception` evaluates to `true`.

questions.question: Which class is at the absolute top of the entire Java class hierarchy?
questions.explanation: In Java, `java.lang.Object` is the root class of all classes, including `Throwable`.

interviewQA.question: Explain the complete hierarchy of exception classes in Java.
interviewQA.answer: At the top is `java.lang.Object`, which is extended by `java.lang.Throwable`. `Throwable` has two direct subclasses: `Error` and `Exception`. `Error` represents critical JVM conditions. `Exception` represents recoverable conditions. Under `Exception`, the class `RuntimeException` marks the boundary: `RuntimeException` and all its subclasses are **unchecked exceptions**, while all other direct subclasses of `Exception` (like `IOException`, `SQLException`) are **checked exceptions**.

interviewQA.question: Why does the compiler prevent placing catch (Exception) before catch (ArithmeticException)?
interviewQA.answer: Java's catch block evaluation is sequential from top to bottom. Because `ArithmeticException` is a subclass of `Exception`, any `ArithmeticException` object would match the first `catch (Exception e)` block. The second block could never be reached under any possible runtime circumstance. Java's compiler strictly rejects unreachable code, flagging a compile-time error.

interviewQA.question: What is the multi-catch feature introduced in Java 7?
interviewQA.answer: Multi-catch allows a single `catch` block to handle multiple unrelated exception types using the pipe operator: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)`. It prevents duplicate catch handler code. Crucially, the alternative exception types in a multi-catch expression must be disjoint (siblings); one cannot be a subclass of another.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions regarding the compiler?
interviewQA.answer: For **checked exceptions**, the compiler enforces the *Catch or Specify* requirement: the code must either enclose the call in a `try-catch` block or declare the exception in the method signature using `throws`. For **unchecked exceptions** (`RuntimeException`), the compiler imposes no enforcement; they may be thrown without explicit declaration.

interviewQA.question: In multi-catch `catch (final IOException | SQLException e)`, is the parameter `e` mutable?
interviewQA.answer: No. In Java multi-catch statements, the exception parameter `e` is implicitly `final`. You cannot reassign `e = new SQLException()` inside a multi-catch block; doing so triggers a compile error.

interviewQA.question: Why did Java designers create the RuntimeException branch?
interviewQA.answer: Unchecked exceptions represent bugs in programming logic (like passing null, illegal arguments, or array index calculation errors) that can occur anywhere in a program. If every possible `NullPointerException` or `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` were checked, every single line of Java code would require verbose try-catch or throws declarations, severely reducing code readability.

interviewQA.question: Can you define your own exception that is unchecked?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. To create a custom unchecked exception, simply extend `java.lang.RuntimeException`. The compiler will treat your custom exception as unchecked, freeing callers from mandatory try-catch blocks.

practiceProblems.title: Demonstrate Specific Before Generic Catch Ordering
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write a try-catch block where 10 is divided by 0. Catch `ArithmeticException` first and print "Specific caught". Add a second catch block for generic `Exception` printing "Generic caught". Verify that only the specific catch executes.
practiceProblems.description: Write a try-catch block where 10 is divided by 0. Catch `ArithmeticException` first and print "Specific caught". Add a second catch block for generic `Exception` printing "Generic caught". Verify that only the specific catch executes.
practiceProblems.hint: Put catch (ArithmeticException e) before catch (Exception e).
hints: Put catch (ArithmeticException e) before catch (Exception e).

practiceProblems.title: Catch Sibling Exceptions via Multi-Catch
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write a method `handleFailures(int test)`. In a try block: if `test == 1` divide by zero; if `test == 2` read `((String)null).length()`. Use a single multi-catch block `catch (ArithmeticException | NullPointerException e)` to print "Caught multi-catch: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName(). Test with test=1 and test=2.
practiceProblems.description: Write a method `handleFailures(int test)`. In a try block: if `test == 1` divide by zero; if `test == 2` read `((String)null).length()`.
